name: Koreamaxxing (surgery tourism)

lead: Koreamaxxing is the looksmaxxing term for going to South Korea to have cosmetic surgery or aesthetic procedures. South Korea has one of the highest per-capita rates of cosmetic surgery in the world, and clinics there are known for eyelid surgery, rhinoplasty and facial contouring. People on looksmaxxing forums describe it as a way to reach hardmaxxing results such as nose tip work or alar base reduction at lower prices than in the West.

The appeal discussed online is price, competition between clinics and routine experience with procedures. Peer-reviewed research looks at cosmetic surgery tourism in general rather than Korea specifically, and documents complications, follow-up difficulty and costs to home health systems.

paras: Forum users describe finding clinics through Korean aggregator apps that list procedures and promotional prices, booking consultations (often in advance online or on arrival), and staying in the country through the early recovery period. Some promotional prices come with an obligation to post a before-and-after review. Users typically combine the trip with a stay of one to several weeks.

Reviews of cosmetic surgery tourism report infections, wound problems and revision surgery after returning home, with limited follow-up from the original surgeon. Korea-specific concerns include "ghost surgery", where a substitute operates in place of the named surgeon; security cameras in operating rooms have been mandatory since 2021. Facial contouring such as V-line surgery carries risks including numbness, according to a maxillofacial surgeon cited in coverage.

chain: Obtain surgery such as eyelid, nose or jaw contouring
angle.text: Koreamaxxers use surgery in Korea to change specific facial features, such as eyelid crease, nose tip or jaw width, often citing lower prices and clinic experience. The appearance change comes from the procedure itself, not from the travel.

lead: Koreamaxxing is a term in looksmaxxing communities for travelling to South Korea to obtain plastic surgery or aesthetic treatments in order to improve facial or body appearance. It sits in the "hardmaxxing" category, since it involves surgical procedures such as double eyelid surgery, rhinoplasty and jaw or cheekbone contouring.[1] People who use it do so to change specific features, such as the eyelid crease, nose tip, jaw angle or cheekbone width, and describe the appeal as lower prices, dense competition between clinics and surgeons who perform these operations routinely.[2]

South Korea has the highest per-capita rate of elective cosmetic surgery in the world according to ISAPS data cited on Wikipedia, and an industry built around foreign patients: 464,452 medical tourists were reported to have visited for cosmetic surgery in 2018, a 16.7 percent rise on 2017.[1] The Korea Times reported about 1.17 million foreign medical tourists in 2024, a record, with dermatology accounting for 56.6 percent of procedures and plastic surgery for 11.4 percent, up 24.3 percent on 2023.[3] A looksmax.org guide on the topic argues that Korea is competitively priced and that every operating room is required to have CCTV.[2]

Published research addresses cosmetic surgery tourism broadly rather than Korea specifically. Reviews describe a growing trend and a complication profile that includes infection, with limited follow-up care for patients who return home.[4][5][6] The wiki documents both sides: what forum users report about Korean clinics, and what the literature on surgery abroad and Korea's own regulatory history say.

paras: Koreamaxxing refers to seeking cosmetic surgery in South Korea, which is widely described as the plastic surgery capital of the world.[1] It is usually discussed by people already considering surgical changes, including non-Asian users who ask whether Korea is a viable destination.[2]

A looksmax.org guide author writes that non-Asians are hesitant to go but that it is "not that big of a deal", that prices are low because of competition and currency, and that clinics can be found through an app called Gangnam Unni.[2] The guide pitches Korea as safer than other low-cost destinations, citing the operating-room CCTV requirement.[2]

sections.h: Background: cosmetic surgery in South Korea
paras: Wikipedia reports that, per a 2012 Economist figure, one in five Korean women had undergone plastic surgery, and that Gallup Korea found support for plastic surgery for marriage rising from 38 percent in 1994 to 66 percent in 2015, while self-reported surgery among women rose from 5 to 31 percent over the same period.[1] It links the trend to social pressure around employment and marriage after the 1997 labour-market changes, the influence of K-pop idols, and older physiognomy traditions.[1] The country is described as holding about a quarter of the international cosmetic industry, with a domestic market valued around US$1.95 billion in 2021.[1]

Popular procedures include double eyelid surgery, with recovery of up to about four weeks; rhinoplasty, described by a 2018 JoongAng report as the most common surgery among ethnic Koreans; and facial contouring such as V-line surgery, which can involve swelling lasting up to six months.[1] The Korea Times lists facial contouring (cheekbone, jaw-angle and chin reshaping), double-jaw surgery, rhinoplasty, liposuction and breast augmentation among what foreign patients seek, and says Seoul has an edge in bone-related surgery.[3]

Patients come from many countries. The Korea Times names Vietnam, Mongolia, the United States, Japan, Russia, Indonesia and China among the main origins, and says 114,074 foreigners visited Seoul for cosmetic enhancements in 2023.[3] Wikipedia credits the global popularity of K-pop and K-drama with part of the growth.[1]

Clinics aimed at foreigners run coordinator teams: one Gangnam clinic profiled by the Korea Times employs about 60 coordinators working in ten languages, handling online consultation, in-person support and post-operative care, and reports foreign patient numbers rising 20 to 30 percent a year since 2022.[3] Seoul Medical Tourism, a city programme, works with 180 medical institutions to help with entry procedures, specialty consultations and appointments, the same article says.[3] The clinic's chief surgeon is quoted as saying word of mouth is what ultimately brings people in.[3] Some clinics also treat revision patients who had complications from procedures done elsewhere.[3]

Wikipedia's article on medical tourism lists South Korea alongside Brazil, Colombia, Costa Rica, Mexico, Turkey and Thailand as a cosmetic surgery destination and describes general travel concerns such as variable follow-up care, limited legal recourse after malpractice abroad, and deep-vein thrombosis risk from flying soon after surgery.[7]

Users on forums describe browsing clinic listings, comparing promotional prices, and arranging consultations. Some event prices come with a requirement to post a review with before-and-after photos, which can often be blurred.[2] Recovery is typically spent in the country, and clinics that serve foreigners describe extra attention to aftercare because follow-up visits are difficult for overseas patients.[3]

Forum members mention procedures such as tip plasty and alar base reduction as reasons to consider Korea.[2] On looksmax.org the topic appears mainly as experience reports and advice from members who have had or are planning surgery there, part of the wider hardmaxxing discussion of surgeries, procedure choice and surgeon selection.[2]

No studies have examined "koreamaxxing" as such. Research on cosmetic surgery tourism in general includes a Journal of Travel Medicine review of the scale of the practice and its complication profile,[4] a legal review noting regulatory and liability gaps,[5] and surveys and cost analyses of patients returning to the US, UK and Ireland with complications after surgery abroad.[8][9][10] A 2011 survey of plastic surgeons found little reported data on outcomes and complication rates for patients treated abroad.[11] A systematic review of breast surgery tourism found the evidence base consists largely of retrospective case series with no defined comparator.[6] Reviews describe infections, including atypical mycobacterial infection after implant surgery, in returning patients: one review pooled 41 reports describing 171 patients, with the incidence rising in developing countries since the start of the millennium.[12] Authors of a regulatory analysis in Health Care Analysis note that financial motives are the most common reason for seeking surgery abroad and examine whether cheaper surgery carries greater risk.[13] These studies are not specific to Korea.

Reviews of surgery abroad cite limited preoperative counselling, non-specialist operators in some destinations, and difficulties with follow-up care and revision.[4][8] The UK NHS cost analysis describes patients presenting to NHS hospitals with complications needing surgery.[9]

In South Korea, "ghost surgery", in which an unlicensed substitute operates while the hired surgeon is absent, has been reported; the Korean Society of Plastic Surgeons estimated about 100,000 victims from 2008 to 2014, and around five patients died during such surgeries from 2014 to 2022, according to Wikipedia. The practice is illegal but rarely prosecuted because evidence is hard to obtain.[1] Lawmakers mandated operating-room cameras in 2021 after public backlash over surgery deaths.[1] V-line surgery carries risks of permanent numbness, according to a maxillofacial surgeon cited there.[1]

Wikipedia also records criticism of Korean beauty standards, including the "escape the corset" movement, and the 2015 shutdown of the reality show Let Me In after complaints that it promoted plastic surgery.[1]

Koreamaxxing sits alongside other travel-for-surgery ideas in hardmaxxing discussion. Proponents frame it as a way of reaching changes that are expensive or hard to book at home, while wider coverage of looksmaxxing, including Wikipedia's article, notes that surgery is the most invasive end of the practice and that surgeons warn of risks from extreme procedures.[2][14]

lore.intro: Koreamaxxing appears on looksmax.org mainly as advice threads from members who have had or are planning surgery there.[2]
